units.text: INT. WOMAN - CONTINUOUS

Caroline, this is Mrs. Arbuthnot, one of my sweetest friends. Lady Caroline Pontefract, Lady Stutfield, Mrs. Allonby, and my young American friend, Miss Worsley, who has just been telling us all how wicked we are.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I am afraid you think I spoke too strongly, Lady Hunstanton. But there are some things in England—
units.name: HESTER

units.text: My dear young lady, there was a great deal of truth, I dare say, in what you said, and you looked very pretty while you said it, which is much more important, Lord Illingworth would tell us. The only point where I thought you were a little hard was about Lady Caroline’s brother, about poor Lord Henry. He is really such good company.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Enter Footman .
Take Mrs. Arbuthnot’s things.
Exit Footman with wraps .
Lady Caroline, I had no idea it was your brother. I am sorry for the pain I must have caused you—I—
units.name: HESTER

units.text: My dear Miss Worsley, the only part of your little speech, if I may so term it, with which I thoroughly agreed, was the part about my brother. Nothing that you could possibly say could be too bad for him. I regard Henry as infamous, absolutely infamous. But I am bound to state, as you were remarking, Jane, that he is excellent company, and he has one of the best cooks in London, and after a good dinner one can forgive anybody, even one’s own relations.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: LADY HUNSTANTON [ to MISS WORSLEY] Now, do come, dear, and make friends with Mrs. Arbuthnot.
She is one of the good, sweet, simple people you told us we never admitted into society.
I am sorry to say Mrs. Arbuthnot comes very rarely to me.
But that is not my fault.
What a bore it is the men staying so long after dinner! I expect they are saying the most dreadful things about us.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Do you really think so?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: I was sure of it.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: How very, very horrid of them! Shall we go onto the terrace?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Oh, anything to get away from the dowagers and the dowdies.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Rises and goes with LADY STUTFIELD to door L.C.
We are only going to look at the stars, Lady Hunstanton.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: You will find a great many, dear, a great many. But don’t catch cold.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: To MRS. ARBUTHNOT.
We shall all miss Gerald so much, dear Mrs. Arbuthnot.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: But has Lord Illingworth really offered to make Gerald his secretary?
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Oh, yes! He has been most charming about it. He has the highest possible opinion of your boy. You don’t know Lord Illingworth, I believe, dear.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I have never met him.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: You know him by name, no doubt?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I am afraid I don’t. I live so much out of the world, and see so few people. I remember hearing years ago of an old Lord Illingworth who lived in Yorkshire, I think.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Ah, yes. That would be the last Earl but one. He was a very curious man. He wanted to marry beneath him. Or wouldn’t, I believe. There was some scandal about it. The present Lord Illingworth is quite different. He is very distinguished. He does—well, he does nothing, which I am afraid our pretty American visitor here thinks very wrong of anybody, and I don’t know that he cares much for the subjects in which you are so interested, dear Mrs. Arbuthnot. Do you think, Caroline, that Lord Illingworth is interested in the Housing of the Poor?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I should fancy not at all, Jane.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: We all have our different tastes, have we not? But Lord Illingworth has a very high position, and there is nothing he couldn’t get if he chose to ask for it. Of course, he is comparatively a young man still, and he has only come to his title within—how long exactly is it, Caroline, since Lord Illingworth succeeded?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: About four years, I think, Jane. I know it was the same year in which my brother had his last exposure in the evening newspapers.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Ah, I remember. That would be about four years ago. Of course, there were a great many people between the present Lord Illingworth and the title, Mrs. Arbuthnot. There was—who was there, Caroline?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: There was poor Margaret’s baby. You remember how anxious she was to have a boy, and it was a boy, but it died, and her husband died shortly afterwards, and she married almost immediately one of Lord Ascot’s sons, who, I am told, beats her.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Ah, that is in the family, dear, that is in the family. And there was also, I remember, a clergyman who wanted to be a lunatic, or a lunatic who wanted to be a clergyman, I forget which, but I know the Court of Chancery investigated the matter, and decided that he was quite sane. And I saw him afterwards at poor Lord Plumstead’s with straws in his hair, or something very odd about him. I can’t recall what. I often regret, Lady Caroline, that dear Lady Cecilia never lived to see her son get the title.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Lady Cecilia?
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Lord Illingworth’s mother, dear Mrs. Arbuthnot, was one of the Duchess of Jerningham’s pretty daughters, and she married Sir Thomas Harford, who wasn’t considered a very good match for her at the time, though he was said to be the handsomest man in London. I knew them all quite intimately, and both the sons, Arthur and George.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: It was the eldest son who succeeded, of course, Lady Hunstanton?
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: No, dear, he was killed in the hunting field. Or was it fishing, Caroline? I forget. But George came in for everything. I always tell him that no younger son has ever had such good luck as he has had.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Lady Hunstanton, I want to speak to Gerald at once. Might I see him? Can he be sent for?
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Certainly, dear. I will send one of the servants into the dining-room to fetch him. I don’t know what keeps the gentlemen so long.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Rings bell .

When I knew Lord Illingworth first as plain George Harford, he was simply a very brilliant young man about town, with not a penny of money except what poor dear Lady Cecilia gave him. She was quite devoted to him. Chiefly, I fancy, because he was on bad terms with his father. Oh, here is the dear Archdeacon.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: To Servant .
It doesn’t matter.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Enter SIR JOHN and DOCTOR DAUBENY.
SIR JOHN goes over to LADY STUTFIELD, DOCTOR DAUBENY to LADY HUNSTANTON.
Lord Illingworth has been most entertaining. I have never enjoyed myself more.
units.name: THE ARCHDEACON

units.text: Sees MRS. ARBUTHNOT.
Ah, Mrs. Arbuthnot.
units.name: THE ARCHDEACON
